prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping holds many neutral atoms for coherent interrogation and has taken optical timekeeping to the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my configuration is unchanged: a single part, B012, to Katori and Ye. What has changed is how I would defend it. The strongest point is not that six members now list it but that nobody in round 1 disputes the science. Eriksson and Danielsson both call the attribution clean and the result mature, and Danielsson says he would not block it. The mechanism is simple and quantitatively understood: at the magic wavelength the lattice light shift cancels to first order, so thousands of atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime without Doppler or recoil shifts. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) reach roughly 1e-18 and compare clocks over fibre, and the millimetre-scale gravitational redshift is a measured laboratory result, not a promise. On the chair's first question, I think the overlap with 2005 and 2012 can be answered in the citation. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb that reads out optical frequencies, and the 2012 prize covered quantum control of single trapped ions. Neither covered holding a large ensemble of neutral atoms in a lattice with the clock transition shifts engineered to cancel, which gives both the stability and the collective, many-body interrogation. The citation should say lattice, magic wavelength and neutral atoms, and should not read as general metrology. On the second and third questions, I would credit Katori for the concept and the early strontium demonstrations and Ye for taking the clock to the accuracy and stability frontier, including the redshift and many-body results, which Olsson and Kroll correctly say belong to his group. I would keep the citation to the invention and realisation of the lattice clock rather than itemise those results, so that the two halves of the credit are covered without a long list. I do not hold a firm view on whether a naming of Lemonde belongs here and I rely on recollection of the 2001 to 2005 record; I would want the committee's secretariat to check that record before the final vote, but I see no evidence in this exchange that anyone proposes a different pair.
statement.case_against: The case against remains lineage and discovery character. Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012) cover neighbouring ground, ion clocks reach comparable accuracy, and Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and Boyd were essential to making lattice clocks work, so a two-name prize is necessarily narrow and will be read by some as leaving out parts of a wide community. Kroll, Lindroth and Mehlig are right that B012 is a measurement capability rather than a discovery about nature, and the headline fundamental-physics payoffs (varying constants, dark matter, a redefined second, clock-based geodesy) are still ahead. I give that real weight, since as a theorist I also want the prize to reward the discovery rather than the application. My answer is that the redshift over millimetres and the 1e-18 agreement between independent clocks are already new, checkable results about nature that were out of reach before, and that the invention is what made them possible. I also accept that my own choice has shifted from B051 in part because I looked at the committee's breadth, and I have tried to test that against the science rather than the count. Finally, the pairing of the 1e-18 result with Ye alone and the concept with Katori alone is a simplification, and a careful citation should not overclaim either half.

responses.point: Kroll supports B012 but says his first place may be a specialist's choice and that he would prefer a result about nature; he also asks whether ion clocks or the ultrastable-laser work behind clock stability should be credited.
responses.response: I agree that the discovery-versus-tool distinction is the most serious scientific objection and I do not think it can be waved away. Where I come down differently is that the question is whether the work opened a regime of nature that could not be observed before, and resolving the gravitational redshift across a millimetre and the 1e-18 clock-to-clock agreement meet that bar. On ion clocks and stabilised lasers, I would not add names. Both are real contributions, but the prize is for the lattice architecture, and adding either would break the three-person limit and blur the citation. I also note your lineage through John Hall's laboratory. Since you report no joint work or financial tie to Katori or Ye, I would record it in the minutes and see no need for recusal, and I would hold the same view for Olsson's University of Tokyo fellowship. For my part, circuit QED lies in my own field and I direct WACQT, so I would defer to colleagues there.

responses.point: Olsson moves B012 to the top, asks that the citation be worded narrowly around the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realisation, and says she cannot settle priority for the early strontium demonstrations from memory.
responses.response: I agree with the narrow wording and have tried to follow it in my citation, naming the lattice, the magic wavelength and neutral atoms and leaving out general statements about timekeeping. I also share your uncertainty about priority among Katori, Lemonde and Takamoto and the JILA teams. I would resolve it as you suggest, by tying Katori to the concept and the first strontium demonstrations and Ye to the realisation at the accuracy frontier, and by having the committee check the dates before the final vote. On timing I side with you and Mehlig: the redefinition of the second is not a criterion, and a prize that waits for a standards-body decision would be rewarding the application. I did list timing as an open uncertainty in round 1, but I now think the demonstrated science stands without it.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B036) is a prediction-then-confirmation story, independently reproduced, that opened a new platform, and that the age of the experiment should not outweigh the surprise.
responses.response: I take that seriously: the Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction followed by correlated insulators and superconductivity is the type of link between calculation and measurement I admire, and I would not oppose B036 in a later year. My reasons for not leading with it now are specific. The pairing mechanism is still unsettled, twist-angle disorder complicates reproducibility, and the experimental credit extends to Cao, Fatemi, Dean and Young beyond the three names supplied, so I could not defend the exact trio. I also defer to condensed-matter colleagues, and in your own file you describe B012 as the safer choice if the committee wants settled understanding. That is where I land for this year.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers the IceCube discovery (B029) because the diffuse neutrino flux is a robust discovery made by nature, but accepts that three names are hard to defend for a collaboration of hundreds and that Baikal and AMANDA complicate the credit.
responses.response: I accept the argument that the diffuse flux is a real discovery by nature and a stronger statement of that criterion than a measurement tool, and I defer to you and the chair on neutrino astronomy since it is outside my field. The difficulty you and Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson all identify is the credit: without evidence on who made the decisive contributions, I could not support naming Halzen, Karle and Spiering. That is the reason I keep it out of my configuration this year and not any doubt about the flux, and I would be willing to look at it again if a defensible set of names emerges.

uncertainties: Whether the 2001 to 2005 priority record for the magic-wavelength concept and the first strontium lattice clocks (Katori, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Ye) supports exactly two names; I rely on recollection and would want it checked.

Whether the committee accepts that the neutral-atom lattice clock is distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which I think depends on how narrowly the citation is worded.
Whether a clock-based redefinition of the second should affect timing; I now lean towards deciding on the demonstrated science alone, but I hold this view with moderate confidence.
Whether recognition of superconducting circuits in 2025 makes B051 unwise this year; I think the overlap is real enough that I keep it only as an alternative, and I am not an impartial judge of it.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. B051 (circuit QED), my opening first choice and a listed alternative, lies in my own research field, and I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, whose Chalmers colleagues work with superconducting-circuit groups. I would defer or recuse on B051, and I would be cautious about B010 because quantum-computing platforms are adjacent to my WACQT role. I have no personal, institutional or collaborative connection to Katori, Ye or the other B012 contributors, so I do not see a conflict on my preferred configuration. I have noted Kroll's lineage through John Hall's laboratory and Olsson's University of Tokyo fellowship and have no objection to their participation.
